intro: Frankfurt bent a subway line rather than lose a lime tree, and in 1907 it hauled a 300-year-old yew across town behind two steam rollers. Five of the twenty-three trees here stand within a few hundred metres of each other in the Westend, around the Palmengarten and Gruneburgpark, which makes that the walk. The rest are out in the districts: ginkgos in Rödelheim and the Bethmannpark, a peace oak of 1871 in Sossenheim, thirty wood-pasture oaks in the Schwanheimer Wald, three village trees in Nieder-Erlenbach, and over the line in Offenbach, three oaks, one planted around 1590.
meta_description: Frankfurt's Naturdenkmal trees: the lime the U-Bahn curves around, a yew moved by steam roller in 1907, and an oak planted around 1590 in Offenbach.
question_answer: Frankfurt's oldest tree is probably the Senckenberg Yew in the Palmengarten, roughly 400 years old: it was already about 300 when two steam rollers moved it across the city in 1907, and local tradition has it planted before the Thirty Years War. The oldest on the city's register with a dated record is the Eschersheimer Linde, a large-leaved lime from the end of the 17th century beside Lindenbaum U-Bahn station. The Schwanheim oaks rival both, a group the city dates to up to 500 years without dating any single trunk.
question_meta: The Senckenberg Yew in the Palmengarten, roughly 400 years old and moved across Frankfurt by steam roller in 1907, is probably the city's oldest tree.
question_context: Frankfurt dates most of its protected trees through a municipal register, which makes the answer checkable and modest. The Senckenberg Yew is the exception: its roughly 400 years rest on an estimate of about 300 at its move in 1907 and a tradition that it was planted before the Thirty Years War, and it is not on the register. The Eschersheimer Linde, from the end of the 17th century, is the oldest tree on the register with a dated record; nobody cored it, so its age is a period rather than a year. The Schwanheim oaks may be older than both: the city gives the group up to 500 years, the register as mirrored on Wikipedia 600 to 1,000, and no single trunk is dated. Offenbach's August Reiss Oak, planted around 1590, is older still, but it stands across the city line. Younger, and dated: the Goethe Ginkgo of about 1750, a copper beech of 1815, a plane of about 1820, a weeping beech of 1845, the Sossenheim peace oak of 1871, and a dawn redwood of about 1950. The eight-stemmed lime in Gruneburgpark and the Ostpark red oak have no age at all. If you know either, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Frankfurt?
faq.a: Probably the Senckenberg Yew in the Palmengarten, roughly 400 years old, which was moved across the city by steam roller in 1907. The oldest on the city's register with a dated record is the Eschersheimer Linde, a large-leaved lime from the end of the 17th century beside Lindenbaum U-Bahn station.

faq.q: Can I see several of Frankfurt's old trees in one walk?
faq.a: Yes. Five of the twenty-three are in the Westend within a few hundred metres of each other: two beeches and the Senckenberg Yew in the Palmengarten, the dawn redwood in the Botanical Garden next door, and the eight-stemmed lime in Gruneburgpark. Bockenheimer Warte is the station for all five. In Nieder-Erlenbach in the far north, the cemetery limes and the oak on An der Bleiche are about 500 metres apart.

faq.q: Are Frankfurt's old trees free to visit?
faq.a: Eighteen of the twenty-three cost nothing and have no gate: the trees on public streets and squares, in Gruneburgpark, the Ostpark, the Bethmannpark, the Bockenheimer Anlage, the Botanical Garden, the Schwanheimer Wald, the Nieder-Erlenbach cemetery, the Offenbach city forest, the Leonhard-Eissnert-Park in Offenbach-Bieber, and a street corner in Offenbach. The two beeches and the Senckenberg Yew are inside the Palmengarten, which sells an admission ticket. The Goethe Ginkgo is free, but the Petrihaus grounds in Rödelheim open only for events and on the last Sunday afternoon of each month from spring to autumn. The oak on An der Bleiche stands on church grounds and is seen from the street.

faq.q: Why does the U-Bahn curve at Lindenbaum?
faq.a: Because the lime was there first and the city kept it. The station carries the tree's name, and the line bends slightly where it stands.

trees.name: The Eschersheimer Linde

location.address: Eschersheimer Landstraße, between Am Lindenbaum and Hinter den Ulmen, Eschersheim

trees.story:
Frankfurt bent a subway line rather than lose this lime. The U-Bahn under Eschersheimer Landstrasse curves slightly where the tree stands, the station beside it is called Lindenbaum, and so is the street. That is a lot of infrastructure named after one large-leaved lime.

It went in at the end of the 17th century as a landmark on what was then an open road out of the city, and it was the smaller of a pair. Locals called it the Kleine Linde, because a bigger Grosse Linde stood nearby until a storm brought that one down in 1923. Around five metres round and some 25 metres tall, it has been a protected natural monument since 1937.

Being a landmark on a road that turned into a city has cost it. The street was paved, the ground around it sealed, and the roots began to suffocate. It got tree surgery in 1955 and again in 1974, drainage in 1968, and by 1984 the city was pumping water and air into the soil around it to keep it alive. Frankfurt has now spent seventy years on life support for a tree it could have removed in an afternoon.

It stands directly on the public street, so there is nothing to pay and nothing to enter. Get off at Lindenbaum station and it is right there, which is the whole point of the name.

best_time.label: June, when it flowers and the pavement under it smells of lime

verified_sources: https://web.archive.org/web/20251028075203/https://frankfurt.de/themen/umwelt-und-gruen/umwelt-und-gruen-a-z/im-gruenen/baeume/naturdenkmale/eschersheimer-linde (city page: Stammumfang circa 5 m, Hoehe circa 25 m, Alter ueber 300 Jahre)
trees.access: Free, standing directly on the public street (Eschersheimer Landstraße), always visible
trees.transport: Lindenbaum U-Bahn station (U1/U2/U3/U8) right beside it; the subway curves around the tree
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing right on the public street, the subway line beneath it curved to spare it. It stands on Eschersheimer Landstraße, at Lindenbaum station.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 011), no. ND 011

trees.name: The Dawn Redwood of the Botanical Garden

location.address: Botanischer Garten Frankfurt, East Asia section, opposite the flat-roof building, right of the bee house, Westend-Nord

trees.story:
Until 1943 this species was known only from fossils. Metasequoia had been described from stone and written off as long extinct, and then living trees turned up in central China and seed went round the world's botanical gardens within a few years. Which means every large dawn redwood in Europe can be dated to within a human lifetime, and this one is among the first of them: it was planted in the Frankfurt Botanical Garden around 1950, as a cutting.

Seventy-five years later its trunk measures 5.72 metres round at chest height, which the German Dendrological Society ranks as the second thickest recorded specimen of its species in the country. It is a conifer that behaves like a broadleaf, putting out soft feathery needles in spring and dropping every one of them in autumn once they have turned rust orange.

It stands in the East Asia section, opposite the flat-roofed building and to the right of the bee house, which is precise enough to walk to. Entry to the Botanical Garden is free. The Palmengarten and its two protected beeches are next door, so the two gardens make a single afternoon, and the city added this tree to its register of natural monuments in 2025.

The odd thing to hold in your head under it: this tree is younger than the news of its own species, and it is already one of the biggest in Germany.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the needles turn rust orange and fall, which is not what a conifer is supposed to do

trees.access: Free. The Botanical Garden is open daily from March to October (March and October 9:00 to 18:00, April to September 9:00 to 19:00) and closed in winter.
trees.transport: Bockenheimer Warte U-Bahn/tram hub, about 10 minute walk; or Westend tram stops closer to the garden entrance
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its soft, feathery needles turning rust orange and dropping entirely each autumn, unlike an evergreen conifer. It stands in the East Asia section of the Botanical Garden.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 010), no. ND 010

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Palmengarten

location.address: Palmengarten Frankfurt, west of the Palmenhaus, by the Gesellschaftshaus, Westend-Süd

trees.story:
This beech has been quietly making more of itself. Where its drooping branches reached the ground they took root, and what began as one tree is now a hall of leaves you can walk into. From outside it reads as a single heavy green dome. From underneath it is a room, held up by the parent trunk and by branch tips that grew themselves legs.

Frankfurt's own tree cadastre dates the planting to 1845. It stands just over four metres round and about 16 metres tall, and a tree surveyor who measured it in June 2023 recorded it as vital with some branch breakage, which is what happens to a weeping beech carrying that much weight sideways. The city put it on its register of natural monuments in 2025.

Weeping beeches are not a wild form. Every one is propagated from a mutant that hangs instead of reaches, so a garden that planted one in 1845 was buying a curiosity, and this is what a curiosity looks like after 180 years of being left alone.

It is in the western part of the Palmengarten by the Gesellschaftshaus, a short walk from the Palmenhaus and from the copper beech that is three decades older again. The Palmengarten charges admission, so this and the copper beech are the two trees on this list you pay to stand under. This one you can also stand inside, which is the better way to do it.

best_time.label: late October and November, when the hall of leaves under it turns copper before it comes down

trees.access: Paid entry to the Palmengarten: regular day ticket 9 euro (10 euro from 16 October 2026 to 7 February 2027). Open daily, March to October 9:00 to 19:00, November to February 9:00 to 16:00; closed only on 24 and 31 December.
trees.transport: Bockenheimer Warte or Westend U-Bahn stations, short walk to the Palmengarten entrance
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its drooping branches rooted where they touch the ground, forming a hollow green room you can walk into. It stands west of the Palmenhaus, by the Gesellschaftshaus.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 013), no. ND 013

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Palmengarten

location.address: Palmengarten Frankfurt, middle section of the park (on the meadow), Westend-Süd

trees.story:
The Palmengarten opened in 1871. This beech was already 56 years old. Frankfurt's tree cadastre dates its planting to 1815, the year of Waterloo, which makes it older than the garden that now charges people to come and look at it.

It is a grafted copper beech, which is how nearly all of them are made. The purple-leaved form does not come reliably true from seed, so a shoot of it is joined onto ordinary green beech rootstock, and on an old specimen you can often still find the join low on the trunk. A surveyor measured it at four and a half metres round in August 2022 and recorded its condition as vital. The city listed it as a natural monument in 2025, under the heading of beauty and rarity, which is an unusually frank thing for a register to write down.

It stands out on the meadow in the middle section of the park with room around it, so the whole low, wide crown is readable at once rather than in pieces through other trees.

Come in late April or May rather than in August. The new leaves open translucent red and only darken through the summer, and by high season the tree has gone almost black-purple and lost half of what makes the walk worth it.

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open translucent red before they darken

trees.access: Paid entry to the Palmengarten: regular day ticket 9 euro (10 euro from 16 October 2026 to 7 February 2027). Open daily, March to October 9:00 to 19:00, November to February 9:00 to 16:00; closed only on 24 and 31 December.
trees.transport: Bockenheimer Warte or Westend U-Bahn stations, short walk to the Palmengarten entrance
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its low, wide crown standing alone on open meadow, leaves opening translucent red before darkening to black-purple. It stands in the middle of the Palmengarten.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 014), no. ND 014

trees.name: The Eight-Stemmed Linden of Grüneburgpark

location.address: Grüneburgpark, at a path crossing in the middle of the park, near the small childrens playground, Westend

trees.story:
Eight trunks come out of the ground here in one tight ring, and they are a single tree. This is a Bündelpflanzung, a bundle planting: several young limes set into one hole so that they grow up together and merge into a single crown. It is deliberate, not an accident of self-seeding, and it is rare enough that Frankfurt made this one a protected natural monument in 2025.

It stands at a path crossing in the middle of the Grüneburgpark, beside the small children's playground, which puts it on everyone's route and almost nobody's list. Walk in among the stems and you are standing inside the tree rather than in front of it, with eight columns around you and one canopy overhead.

Nobody has established how old it is. No published record we can find carries a planting date, and the designation does not give one either, so this page does not guess. The same goes for which lime it is: small-leaved, large-leaved and the hybrid between them are close enough that neither source commits, and we are not going to commit for them.

If you know either answer, from a park archive, an old photograph or a plaque we have missed, tell us and it goes on the page. Meanwhile the park is free, open at all hours, and the tree is unmistakable once you are looking for eight of anything.
trees.access: Free, public park (Grüneburgpark), open at all times
trees.transport: Miquel-/Adickesallee or Holzhausenstraße bus/tram stops; about 10-15 minute walk from Bockenheimer Warte U-Bahn
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its eight trunks rising in one tight ring from a single planting, hollow enough to stand inside. It stands at a path crossing in the middle of Grüneburgpark.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 020), no. ND 020

best_time.label: late June, when the eight stems of the Grüneburgpark linden flower together, heavily scented and loud with bees

trees.name: The Plane Tree at the Nebbiensches Gartenhaus

location.address: Bockenheimer Anlage, behind the Nebbiensches Gartenhaus, Innenstadt

trees.story:
Seven metres and thirteen centimetres around the trunk, measured in October 2025. That is a plane tree you could not reach a tenth of the way around, standing in a strip of park a few minutes from Frankfurt's opera house. An independent big-tree survey recorded 713 centimetres last autumn; another surveyor measured 704 in 2022. Two measurements three years apart agreeing that closely is the kind of number worth trusting.

It was planted in 1820, ten years after the neoclassical pavilion it stands behind, the Nebbiensches Gartenhaus. Both sit in the Bockenheimer Anlage, part of the ring of parkland Frankfurt laid out on the ground where its city walls had stood, which is why the green in this part of town runs in a curve instead of a grid. The tree is around 35 metres tall with a crown some 26 metres across, and it carries entry 028 on the city's register of natural monuments.

Two centuries is not particularly old for a plane. It is old for this address, where a garden pavilion from 1810 now sits in sight of the banking towers.

Access is free and unrestricted at any hour, which is worth saying because two of the protected trees on this list stand behind an admission desk. This one is simply in a public park, and you can put your hand on it.
trees.access: Free, public park (Bockenheimer Anlage), unrestricted access confirmed by an October 2025 independent tree survey
trees.transport: Alte Oper or Bockenheimer Warte U-Bahn stations, a few minutes walk through the Anlagenring park
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, 7.13 metres round, standing directly behind the neoclassical Nebbiensches Gartenhaus. It stands in the Bockenheimer Anlage.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 028), no. ND 028

trees.name: The Goethe Ginkgo of Roedelheim

location.address: Petrihaus, Alt-Roedelheim, 60489 Frankfurt am Main

trees.story:
In September 1815 Goethe wrote a poem about a single ginkgo leaf, split down the middle and still one leaf, and sent it to Marianne von Willemer with two real ginkgo leaves fixed to the page. Rödelheim would like those leaves to have come from this tree. It has a case, and it does not have proof.

The ginkgo went in around 1750 beside the Petrihaus, in what was then the little County of Solms-Rödelheim. The house later belonged to the banker Georg Brentano, and in September 1814 Goethe was a guest of the Brentano family in Rödelheim. A year later came 'Gingo biloba'. The board at the tree suggests the connection. Wikipedia calls it possible and says the leaves cannot be traced to this tree with certainty, which is where the evidence stops, and so does this page.

The tree needs no poem. The city register gives it about 260 years and 18 metres; the Wikipedia article says over 270 and calls it the oldest ginkgo in Germany, which is that article's claim rather than ours. It stands a few metres south of the Petrihaus, with the Nidda weir just beyond and Brentanopark on the far bank.

The catch is the gate. The grounds open only for events of the Förderverein Petrihaus and on the last Sunday afternoon of each month from spring to autumn, so check before you go. The newest dated photograph we found is from 2017; if you have stood under it since, tell us.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn gold

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_Frankfurt_am_Main (ND 021: about 260 years old, 18 m high; cites the city page)
trees.access: Stands in the grounds of the Petrihaus, which are open to the public only at events of the Foerderverein Petrihaus and on the afternoon of the last Sunday of each month from spring to autumn (per de.wikipedia). Outside those times the tree is not reachable; check the Foerderverein before going.
trees.transport: S-Bahn S3, S4, S5 to Frankfurt-Roedelheim, about 500 m (7 min walk); bus 34 or 72 to Alt-Roedelheim, a few metres away.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one ginkgo in the Petrihaus grounds, about 18 metres tall, with fan-shaped leaves split down the middle. It stands a few metres south of the house, between it and the Nidda weir.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 021), no. ND 021

trees.name: The Paradieseiche of Sachsenhausen

location.address: Corner of Oberer Schafhofweg and Saechsenhaeuser Landwehrweg, 60599 Frankfurt am Main

trees.story:
Frankfurt protects this oak for two reasons, and one of them is a beetle. The city's register entry 035 lists the tree's rare, striking form, and then adds that it is habitat for the stag beetle, a protected species that depends on old oaks.

It was not always the main event. The city's own description says it was once just one oak among many in the Stadtwald, the city forest on Frankfurt's south side, and is now a solitary tree that shapes the landscape around it. Somewhere along the way people started calling it the Paradieseiche, the Paradise Oak. The city records the nickname and does not explain it. If you know where it comes from, tell us.

The numbers are the city's own. It is 140 to 160 years old, which puts it in the second half of the 19th century, with a trunk about 4.2 metres round, a crown about 20 metres across and a height of 25 metres. For an oak of that age, that is a lot of tree.

It stands at the corner of Oberer Schafhofweg and Sachsenhäuser Landwehrweg, on the forest edge in Sachsenhausen-Süd, and you see it from the road. There is nothing to pay and no gate, and a protected zone of 20 metres runs around the trunk.
verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_Frankfurt_am_Main (ND 035: 140 to 160 years old, 25 m high, Stammumfang 4.20 m; cites the city page)
trees.access: Free. Stands at a street corner on the edge of the Stadtwald; visible from the public roads. Protected zone of 20 m around the tree.
trees.transport: Not verified; Sachsenhausen-Sued, roughly 2 km south of the Sachsenhausen centre. Check RMV for the nearest stop.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone big oak at the street corner, about 25 metres tall with a trunk 4.2 metres round, standing apart from the forest. It stands where Oberer Schafhofweg meets Sachsenhäuser Landwehrweg.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 035), no. ND 035

trees.name: The Schwanheim Old Oaks

location.address: Alteichen-Pfad, Schwanheimer Wald, 60529 Frankfurt am Main

trees.story:
Until the 1920s, pigs were driven into this wood to feed under these oaks, and in the Middle Ages sheep, goats, horses and cattle grazed here too. That is the whole explanation for the place: about thirty pedunculate oaks that grew up on open, grazed ground rather than packed into a forest, which is what wood-pasture means.

Germany was once full of it. From the 18th century most of it was replaced with spruce plantations, and what survived became a favourite subject for the painters of the Kronberg colony. One of them, Fritz Wucherer, painted 'Bei den Schwanheimer Eichen' in 1899, showing a conspicuous oak whose trunk forks in two. A large reproduction stands on the path, so you can compare the painting with the trees.

How old they are depends on which official text you read. The city's own page says up to 500 years; the register as mirrored on German Wikipedia says 600 to 1,000. Several centuries is as far as the sources agree. They are only 12 to 16 metres tall, and the trunks average about 2.75 metres round.

The thickest carries thumb-thick galleries bored by the great capricorn beetle, and woodpeckers come for the larvae. Not all the news is good. For some years the oaks have been suffering from climate change, their crowns thinning and branches dying, and some of the group is already dead wood.

The Alteichen-Pfad, part of Frankfurt's GrünGürtel, runs through the group. It is open forest, and free.
trees.access: Free. Open forest path (the Alteichen-Pfad, part of the Frankfurt GruenGuertel) through the group, with information stelae.
trees.transport: Not verified; Schwanheim in the southwest of Frankfurt, reached on foot from the district through the Schwanheimer Wald. Check RMV for the nearest stop.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the group of about thirty old oaks along the Alteichen-Pfad, with information stelae and a large reproduction of Wucherer's 1899 painting beside the path. They stand in the Schwanheimer Wald.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 030), no. ND 030

trees.name: The Peace Oak of Sossenheim

location.address: Wiesenfeldweg, 65936 Frankfurt am Main

trees.story:
Lightning once split this oak from its crown to its roots, and it is still standing. The crack is part of the city's own description of the tree, entry 022 on Frankfurt's register of natural monuments.

It was planted in 1871 to mark the peace that ended the Franco-Prussian War, which makes it a Friedenseiche, a peace oak, put in the ground in the same year the German Empire was proclaimed. That gives it something most old trees lack: a known birthday, and an age of about 150 years that nobody had to estimate.

It also stands on an old line. Sossenheim was a village before it was part of Frankfurt, and until about 1800 it was closed in by a Haingraben, a fence and hedge with a ditch along it. The oak stands where the village edge used to be. Today that edge is the Wiesenfeldweg, between housing and allotment gardens, and the tree has outlasted both the Empire it was planted under and the peace it was planted for.

It is 4.60 metres round and about 18 metres tall, a broad trunk for a century and a half. The city does not say whether the lightning crack is weakening it, and we will not guess. The newest dated photograph we have found is from 2020; if you have walked past since, tell us how it looks.

It is free, and seen from the public way at the southern edge of Sossenheim.
verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkmale_in_Frankfurt_am_Main (ND 022: planted 1871, 18 m high, Stammumfang 4.60 m; cites the city page)
trees.access: Free. Stands on the Wiesenfeldweg at the southern edge of Sossenheim, between housing and allotment gardens; seen from the public way. Protected zone of 20 m.
trees.transport: Not verified; southern edge of Sossenheim. Check RMV for the nearest stop.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.60 metres round, and the lightning crack the city records from crown to roots. It stands on the Wiesenfeldweg at the southern edge of Sossenheim, between the houses and the allotments.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 022), no. ND 022

trees.name: The Castle Square Oak of Hoechst

location.address: Hoechster Schlossplatz, in front of the Zollhaus, 65929 Frankfurt am Main

trees.story:
Frankfurt's register entry for this oak says it is still fairly young and has not reached its full size, which is a candid thing to write into the document that protects it. It is over 150 years old, about 13 metres tall and 2.6 metres round. None of that is a record. What it has is the square.

The Höchster Schlossplatz sits in the tight old town of Höchst, beside the castle on the Main, and the city's own text calls the oak the formative centre of the place. Its crown spreads about 21 metres, wider than the tree is tall, over a square closed in by old buildings. A wooden bench runs in a ring around the trunk, which tells you what the square thinks the tree is for.

It stands in front of the entrance to the Zollhaus, and it was already here when Höchst was still a town of its own. Frankfurt only absorbed it in 1928, so this oak has been the middle of the square under two different town halls. Today the city protects it as natural monument 024, with a zone of ten metres around the trunk.

So come for the place rather than the measurements. There is nothing to pay and nothing to find: walk into the square, look for the bench, and sit on it.

trees.access: Free. On the public Hoechster Schlossplatz in the old town, in front of the Zollhaus entrance; a wooden bench rings the trunk.
trees.transport: Not verified; Hoechst old town, beside the Hoechst Schloss on the Main. Check RMV (Hoechst S-Bahn is in the district).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wooden bench built in a ring around its trunk. It stands on the Höchster Schlossplatz, in front of the entrance to the Zollhaus.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmale der Stadt Frankfurt am Main (ND 024), no. ND 024

trees.name: The Senckenberg Yew

location.address: Palmengarten, north-eastern edge, south of the playground and north of a greenhouse

trees.story:
In 1907 two steam rollers dragged this yew three and a half kilometres across Frankfurt, its roots boxed in a block of earth that weighed about 45 tonnes.

For three centuries it had grown in the garden at the Eschenheimer Turm that the physician Johann Christian Senckenberg bought in 1766: his botanical garden, with his hospital and anatomy beside it and later a library and museum. When the Senckenberg foundation sold the site in 1907, its administrators asked for two things to be kept. One was Senckenberg's tomb. The other was this tree.

Keeping the tree took three years. On the advice of an English specialist in moving old trees, the main roots were trenched and cut back so that new ones would form at the stumps. The rootball came out 4.5 metres square and 2 metres deep, was boxed in timber and set on rollers, and between late May and June it crossed the city. Philipp Holzmann's firm did the work, the public was asked for money and the city council paid in. Frankfurt's city history institute says no tree that old and that big had ever been moved so far.

Roughly 400 years is the best figure. The institute put it at about 300 at the time of the move, and local tradition has it planted before the Thirty Years War. German Wikipedia counts it among the oldest yews in the country.

It joined the Palmengarten in 1960, so seeing it costs a ticket.

trees.transport: Bockenheimer Warte or Westend U-Bahn stations, short walk to the Palmengarten entrance
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the information boards at the tree, which tell the story of its 1907 move. It stands at the north-eastern edge of the Palmengarten, south of the playground and north of a greenhouse.

trees.name: The Red Oak of the Ostpark

location.address: Ostpark, north-eastern end, Frankfurt-Ostend

trees.story:
In October 2025 Frankfurt went through its register of natural monuments and struck off a long list of entries. This red oak stayed. The revised register keeps it as natural monument 025 and gives its reasons in three words: rarity, character and beauty.

Those three words are close to everything on record. The register lists no age, no girth and no height for it, and no source we have found says when it was planted or by whom. What can be said is short. It is a northern red oak, a species from eastern North America, standing at the north-eastern end of the Ostpark in Ostend. Somebody logged it nearby in May 2024, and a photograph taken in November 2025 shows it at that end of the park, still standing after the cull of the register.

The species is the reason to come in autumn. Red oaks were planted across Europe for the colour their leaves turn, a rich red that Frankfurt's native oaks do not manage, and the lobes of each leaf end in fine bristles where a pedunculate oak's are rounded.

The Ostpark is a free public city park. The pin is approximate, so head for the park's north-eastern end and look for the oak with the pointed leaves. Nobody has published how old or how big this tree is. If you have stood under it with a tape measure, or know when it went in, tell us.

trees.name: The Cemetery Lindens of Nieder-Erlenbach

location.address: Friedhof Nieder-Erlenbach (cemetery entrance), Frankfurt-Nieder-Erlenbach

trees.story:
Frankfurt's register says there are three small-leaved limes at this cemetery. The newest photograph we have found, taken at the entrance in June 2020, shows two. Either the third stands out of the frame or it has gone, and nothing we have read settles which. If you go, count them and tell us.

The register line itself is plain: three Winterlinden over 100 years old on the cemetery of Nieder-Erlenbach. They are natural monument 036, protected for rarity, character and beauty, and they came through the October 2025 revision of the register, which removed many other entries. So as recently as 2025 the city still thought the group worth keeping.

That is all that is written down. No girth, no height, and an age that is a floor rather than a figure: over a century, and nobody has published a closer date, or who planted them by the gate.

Small-leaved limes flower late, in July, after the other limes have finished. That is the month to come, when the entrance smells of them.

Nieder-Erlenbach is in Frankfurt's far north, about 15 kilometres from the centre. The cemetery is free to enter. About 500 metres east, in front of the Protestant church's community house, stands a protected oak 4.55 metres round, so the two make a short village walk.

best_time.label: July, when the limes flower late and scent the cemetery gate

trees.name: The Oak on An der Bleiche, Nieder-Erlenbach

location.address: An der Bleiche 8, in front of the Gemeindehaus of the Protestant church, Frankfurt-Nieder-Erlenbach

trees.story:
This oak is 4.55 metres round, and the document that protects it will only say it is over 100 years old. That gap between the tape measure and the date is the most interesting thing on record about it.

It is natural monument 037 on Frankfurt's register, listed for its character and beauty, and it was kept when the city revised the register in October 2025 and deleted many other entries. The register gives the girth and the floor of the age and nothing else: no height, no planting date, no story. Nobody has published a closer figure, and we will not invent one from the girth.

It stands in front of the community house of the Protestant church at An der Bleiche 8 in Nieder-Erlenbach, on ground that belongs to the Protestant regional association. No source we have found says those grounds are open, so treat it as a tree to look at from the street, which is where the pin is. The newest photograph we know of is from January 2021. If you pass it, or know when it was planted, tell us.

Nieder-Erlenbach is a village district in Frankfurt's far north, about 15 kilometres from the centre. The protected cemetery limes are about 500 metres west, which makes the pair a short walk through the village.

trees.name: The Chestnut at the Schaeferkoeppel

location.address: Am Schaeferkoeppel, Frankfurt-Nieder-Erlenbach

trees.story:
By the register's figures this horse chestnut put on more than five metres of trunk in about 110 years. Frankfurt lists it at 5.30 metres round and 17 metres tall, and that is a great deal of girth for the age. Both numbers come from the same city entry and we print them as the city does, but one of them may be generous. If you know which, tell us.

It is natural monument 032, and the register gives three reasons for keeping it: its character, its beauty and what the register calls landeskundliche Gründe, roughly reasons of regional history and geography. The entry does not say what that history is. It came through the October 2025 revision of the register, which deleted many other trees, and a photograph from June 2020 shows it standing at Am Schäferköppel, on the northern edge of Nieder-Erlenbach, the northernmost district of Frankfurt and about 20 kilometres from the centre.

How you reach it is the thin part. Nothing we have read says whether it stands on the edge of a public path or in a field, so the pin is the register's coordinate and nothing finer. If the ground turns out to be farmland, look at it from the road and leave the field alone.

Come in May, when horse chestnuts hold white candles upright over the whole crown. The cemetery limes and the oak on An der Bleiche are about two kilometres south, in the village.

trees.name: The August Reiss Oak of Offenbach

location.address: Offenbach city forest, on the forest route near the Pechschneise, about 300 m east of the road to Dietzenbach, Offenbach am Main (day trip from Frankfurt)

trees.story:
This oak was planted around 1590, which makes it older than the Thirty Years War and, by the City of Offenbach's own count, the oldest tree in Offenbach. The city's forest route and a 1979 survey of its natural monuments agree on the date.

It is also tall: over 40 metres by the city, about 40 by the survey, near the top of what a pedunculate oak reaches, and nobody has published a newer measurement. The trunk is almost two metres across. That works out at roughly six metres round, which is our arithmetic from the diameter, not anyone's tape.

The name honours August Reiss, 1844 to 1929, forestry inspector of the princely Isenburg forests from 1874 to 1927. When he started, the oak was nearly three hundred.

The oak is stop 10 on Offenbach's signed Waldroute, on the path over the bridge near the Pechschneise, about 300 metres east of the road to Dietzenbach. The city warns that bushes have grown up around it. The forest is free, with no gate. The list of Offenbach's natural monuments records two other oaks as gone, one fallen and one felled in 2019, and the newest photograph of this one is from August 2020; if you have seen it since, tell us.

Offenbach is its own city, an S-Bahn ride from Frankfurt, and the oak is a forest walk of about three kilometres south of its centre. Check RMV for the journey.

trees.name: The Service Tree of Riedberg

location.address: Graf-von-Stauffenberg-Allee, small meadow at the Niederurseler Hang, 60438 Frankfurt am Main

official_register.name: Frankfurt am Main Naturdenkmale, entry 001 (2025 list)

trees.access: Free; open meadow beside the public street Graf-von-Stauffenberg-Allee (Baumkunde register: 'oeffentlich zugaenglich'). Protected site is a 15 m radius around the trunk.
trees.transport: Western edge of Riedberg, Frankfurt U-Bahn area; nearest stop and walk time not measured
trees.story:
In 2020 two conservation groups, NABU and BUND, put up a stele for this tree's hundredth birthday. The volunteer register that reports the party also gives its planting year as 1896, which would have made it 124 on the day. Neither date comes with a paper trail we could read, so the honest age is somewhere between 100 and 130 years.

The species is not in doubt. This is a Speierling, a service tree, one of Germany's rare native fruit trees, and it stands alone on a small meadow at the Niederurseler Hang. Frankfurt's 2025 list of natural monuments puts it first, as entry 001, for its rarity, its character and its beauty.

It is still putting on wood. Volunteers measured the trunk at 2.71 metres round in 2015 and 2.89 metres in 2022, when they found it 15 metres tall and in vital health. In September and October it carries small fruit shaped like apples or pears, sweet only once they soften.

One loose end. The description of a 2020 photograph on Wikimedia Commons says the tree was designated in January 2014 and no longer was by 2020. The city's 2025 list, the newer word, still carries it.

The meadow is free and open, beside Graf-von-Stauffenberg-Allee on the western edge of Riedberg. The protected ground is the circle within 15 metres of the trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only tree on its small meadow, a service tree about 15 metres tall with a trunk 2.89 metres round. It stands beside Graf-von-Stauffenberg-Allee at the Niederurseler Hang.

best_time.label: September and October, when the small apple- and pear-shaped fruit ripen

trees.name: The Border Oak at Berger Warte

location.address: Vilbeler Landstrasse (B521), forest track entrance beside the Seckbacher Busch, at the Frankfurt / Bad Vilbel boundary near the Berger Warte
location.neighbourhood: Seckbacher Busch, Bad Vilbel (Frankfurt city boundary, Berger Rücken)

official_register.name: Wetteraukreis Naturdenkmale, ND 440.142 'Eiche (am Seckbacher Busch)', Bad Vilbel, list status May 2020

trees.access: Free; stands at the mouth of a forest track at the edge of the B521 (Vilbeler Landstrasse) beside a prefab-house showroom, marked with a red plaque 'Abteilung 2 Seckbacher Busch'. Roadside, no entry needed; busy road, so approach from the track.
trees.transport: Between Frankfurt-Bergen and Bad Vilbel, about 6 km north-east of Frankfurt centre; nearest bus stop and walk time not measured
trees.story:
Citizen surveyors counted 51 old oaks around Enkheim and Bergen in 2016. This is the only one of them designated a natural monument, and its near twin stands unmarked on the other side of the road.

The pair flank the B521 where it leaves the Vilbeler Wald, about 300 metres north-west of the old Jewish cemetery of Bergen. The surveyors put a tape round both at chest height and got 4.00 and 4.10 metres, without saying which is which. Their rule of thumb for forest oaks turns that girth into a germination date around 1700: an estimate from size, not a count of rings, so call it somewhere between 250 and 330 years. Senckenberg staff told the Frankfurter Neue Presse that oaks this old are otherwise known only in the Schwanheim forest.

Five metres away stands a boundary stone carved GH, for the Grand Duchy of Hesse. The survey suggests that could make this an old border oak. It is a suggestion, not a finding.

The protection comes from the Wetteraukreis, because the tree stands just inside Bad Vilbel, on Frankfurt's city line. Its register entry, natural monument 440.142, is named for the Seckbacher Busch, as is the red plaque on the tree, but no shared coordinate ties the register to the surveyors' oak, so the match is very likely rather than proven.

Nobody says whether it is pedunculate or sessile; if you can tell, tell us. The latest dated photograph is from 2018.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the red plaque reading 'Abteilung 2 Seckbacher Busch' and a GH boundary stone five metres off. It stands at the mouth of a forest track beside the B521, next to a prefab-house showroom.
trees.verify_notes: PHOTO IN HAND (for the photo lane): Commons 'Bad Vilbel, Eiche am Seckbacher Busch.jpg', Karsten Ratzke (User:Karsten11), CC0, taken 2018-07-03, no geotag. It is Wikidata Q125389854's image. Facts seen on fetched pages: (1) de.wikipedia 'Enkheimer Alteichen' (article by the citizen surveyors, uses their 2016 tape measurements at 1.30 m): two outstanding oaks on the Berger Rücken either side of the B521 at the edge of the Vilbeler Wald, about 300 m north-west of the old Jewish cemetery Bergen, girths 4.00 and 4.10 m, germinated around 1700 by the survey's age formula (girth x 0.8 for forest oaks, so an estimate, not a core). One of the two, at the mouth of a forest track next to a prefab-house centre and carrying a red plaque 'Abteilung 2 Seckbacher Busch', is the ONLY tree of the whole Enkheim and Bergen old-oak stand that is a designated Naturdenkmal; the other, across the road, is nearly identical and unmarked (candidate second lead, same spot). A boundary stone with the initials GH (Grand Duchy of Hesse) stands 5 m from the tree, which the article says could mean an old boundary oak; this is the article's suggestion, not established. Which of 4.00 or 4.10 m belongs to the designated tree is not stated, so 4.1 is recorded as the upper figure. (2) FNP 2016-10-25 article (fetched) independently reports the survey and names the thickest of 51 oaks then found as 4.46 m; Senckenberg staff in it say comparably old oaks are known only in the Schwanheim forest. Register: Wetteraukreis ND list May 2020 (PDF unreadable here, text not extracted), number and name taken from a search result and from Wikidata Q125389854 (P1435 citing that PDF, P625 50.162933, 8.735679), Wikipedia 'Liste der Naturdenkmaeler in Bad Vilbel' lists it in Flur 13 at about the same coordinate, protection for being an old tree, no size data. IDENTITY CAUTION: the match between the register entry and the oak the survey describes rests on the shared name 'Seckbacher Busch' and the plaque text, not on a shared coordinate; the survey article gives no coordinate for the Berger Warte pair. Hence pin approximate. Species: article says all surveyed oaks are Pedunculate or Sessile, not which, so genus only. Age derived and broad (girth 4.0 to 4.1 m, forest-oak factor 0.8 gives roughly 320 to 330 years, article says around 1700); lifecheck NONE for the coordinate, last dated evidence the 2018 photo and the 2016 survey, so alive is thin. Note it stands in Bad Vilbel (Wetteraukreis), a different municipality from Frankfurt, but at the city boundary, about 6 km from the centre. Register-only plus one survey source, flagged.

trees.name: The Brentanopark Oak

location.address: Brentanopark, Roedelheim, 60489 Frankfurt am Main

trees.access: Free; the oak stands in the middle of the Brentanopark, a public park owned by the city of Frankfurt since 1926 (monumentale-eichen.de); Baumkunde register lists access as public.
trees.transport: S-Bahn S3, S4, S5 to Frankfurt-Roedelheim (the Petrihaus ginkgo frk_007, 150 m away, is given as about 500 m from the station); exact walk to the oak not measured
trees.story:
This oak is getting thinner. Volunteer measurers found its waist at 6.97 metres in 2019 and 6.90 metres two years later, and the bark that has come away in large patches accounts for about eight centimetres of the loss. Even so, nearly seven metres round is a great deal of pedunculate oak.

It has lost height too. The crown stood 28 metres until it was cut back a few years before 2021; it now measures 25 to 26 metres, with a spread of about 25. The first branches leave the trunk at two metres, and the stubs of others, sawn off long ago, have almost grown over.

The measurers put it at about 300 years, an estimate from its size, so read that as somewhere between 250 and 350. The Brentanopark around it was laid out in 1770 and extended in 1823; nobody has recorded whether the oak was planted for the park or was already standing. The city has owned it since 1926 and rebuilt it for the public.

Its health is the honest worry. In 2021 its vitality seemed to be declining, and the register visit of July 2026 recorded it as ill, with bark damage. It was alive and photographed that month.

It stands in the middle of the park, free to visit, in Rödelheim. The S3, S4 and S5 stop at Frankfurt-Rödelheim, and the Petrihaus ginkgo is about 150 metres away, which makes the two a single stop.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 6.9 metres round, with bark missing in large patches and old sawn-off branch stubs almost grown over. It stands in the middle of the Brentanopark, about 150 metres from the Petrihaus ginkgo.
trees.verify_notes: Facts seen on two fetched pages, both volunteer measurers (no official register, so flagged; neither is a finding aid or monumentaltrees.com). (1) monumentale-eichen.de (Rainer Lippert, measured 2021, page updated 2021-10-21): Pedunculate oak, 'about 300 years', breast-height girth 6.90 m, waist girth 6.80 m, height 26 m, crown spread 25 m; first branches at 2 m; trunk shows several sawn-off branch stubs almost fully overgrown; bark missing in large patches; crown was reduced a few years ago and stood 28 m before; condition 'still quite good, vitality seems to be declining'; coordinate 50.124379, 8.615942. Park laid out 1770, extended 1823, owned by the city since 1926 and rebuilt for the public. (2) Baumkunde register 1175 (updated 2026-07-10, last visit and measurement 2026-07-05, observers incl. Baumradler, Rainer Lippert, Palme): girth 6.9 m (waist girth 6.88 m in 2017, 6.97 m in 2019, 6.90 m in 2021, bark loss has cost about 8 cm), height 25 m, age 300 (an estimate), 'Zustand: krank, Borkenschaden' (ill, bark damage), photos dated up to July 2026 so it is ALIVE now, but declining; coordinate 50.12428, 8.61602 (about 12 m from the Lippert point). Park/oak age caution: the park's 1770 founding is NOT a date for this tree; 300 years is the measurers' estimate and Lippert's page gives the method on its 'Alter' page (not read), so age is kept broad 250 to 350. Girth of 6.9 m is large for a Pedunculate oak; the reading is consistent across five measurements 2017 to 2026, so not a corrupt field. Pin: two independent GPS positions of the measurers within 12 m, a single monumental oak in the middle of the park, so confirmed. Same park as the Petrihaus ginkgo (frk_007, 50.123927, 8.613951, about 150 m away): a two-tree stop. Nearby but separate: the Baumkunde register 7325 'Eiche am Brentano Bad' (Pedunculate, girth 6.12 m in 2020, 22 m, about 300 years, 50.12604, 8.62003) stands on the grounds of the Frankfurter Sportjugend, access 'Privatgelaende', cut back hard in May 2024: NOT delivered (private grounds), recorded here as a lead. Nothing here is fabricated beyond these two pages; frankfurt.de does not list it as a Naturdenkmal in the 2025 list I read.

trees.name: The Jahn Oak of Offenbach

location.address: Corner of Gutenbergstrasse and Starkenburgring, Offenbach am Main

official_register.name: Offenbach am Main Naturdenkmal no. 11 (Wikipedia mirror of the city list, citing the 88th Bericht des Offenbacher Vereins fuer Naturkunde, 1988)

trees.story:
This oak was planted for the hundredth birthday of a sports ground in Berlin. In 1811 the first German Turnplatz, an open-air gymnastics ground, opened in the Hasenheide, and a century later the gymnasts of Offenbach marked the date with a tree. A low stone at the trunk still says so: in memory of the opening of the first German Turnplatz in the Hasenheide in Berlin, 1811, 19 June, 1911.

The planting followed a gymnastics display on the Bieberer Berg, after which every club in Offenbach and Bürgel merged into the Offenbacher Turnerschaft. The register dates it to the winter of 1911 to 1912, so it is about 115 years old.

Then the oak took on a heavier job. On 10 August 1928, the 150th birthday of the gymnastics pioneer Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, whose name it carries, a second stone was unveiled beside it: a pyramid-shaped boulder brought from the Taunus, for 211 club members killed in the First World War. Its metal plaque has since gone. The scars where it was fixed have not.

The tree is no giant: a wide, well-formed crown marking a road junction, made natural monument number 11 in July 1988. Nobody has published its girth or height, and the newest dated photograph we know of is from 2018. If you have put a tape round it, tell us.

It stands on the corner of Gutenbergstraße and Starkenburgring in Offenbach, free and on public ground, an S-Bahn ride from Frankfurt.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two stones at its foot: a low inscribed stone at the trunk and a pyramid-shaped boulder with the scars of a lost plaque. It stands on the corner of Gutenbergstraße and Starkenburgring.

trees.name: The Great Oak of the Leonhard-Eissnert-Park

location.address: Leonhard-Eissnert-Park, Offenbach-Bieberer Berg

trees.access: Free, public park (Leonhard-Eissnert-Park), open at all times per flurbaum.de ('Zugang: unbeschraenkt moeglich (oeffentlich)'); the tree is on a meadow in the park.
trees.transport: Not verified: Offenbach-Bieber S-Bahn station is in the same district as the Bieberer Berg park; the walk from there and the travel time from Frankfurt were not checked.
trees.story:
Two careful people have measured this oak, and they cannot agree what it is. One says sessile oak, about 380 years old, which would put its first shoot around 1650, soon after the Thirty Years War. The other says pedunculate oak, about 200. That is a gap of nearly two centuries on the same trunk.

Neither is an official register, and Offenbach's list of natural monuments does not include it. Both are private surveyors who date their visits. Flurbaum.de, in May 2026, measured it at 6.08 metres round at 1.30 metres up and about 30 metres tall, with a crown about as wide, and describes the trunk as three-stemmed. Rainer Lippert's Monumentale Eichen list, updated in March 2022, gives 5.91 metres at the waist and 27 metres tall. Measuring at different heights explains the girth. Nothing on record explains the age, so we give the whole range and call it an oak. If you know which oak it is, tell us.

Either way it was already old in 1911, when Leonhard Eissnert began laying out a woodland park here on the Bieberer Berg. It stands on a meadow in that park, free and open at all hours. The May 2026 visit found some lower branches sawn off and recorded no dieback.

The park is in Offenbach-Bieber, part of Offenbach am Main, the separate city on Frankfurt's eastern edge. Offenbach-Bieber has its own S-Bahn station; check RMV for the walk from there.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about six metres round, on a meadow, with some lower branches sawn off. It stands in the Leonhard-Eissnert-Park on the Bieberer Berg in Offenbach.
trees.verify_notes: Two independent private measurers, both with dated measurements and near-identical coordinates, no official register. (1) flurbaum.de 'Starke Baeume in Frankfurt am Main' (Stand Mai 2026): Traubeneiche (Quercus petraea), three stems, girth 608 cm at 130 cm, height about 30 m, crown about 30 m, 'im Jahr der Messung geschaetzt 380 Jahre alt, demnach um 1650 gekeimt', meadow/park, flat, 122 m elevation, coordinates 50.0974, 8.7943, damage: some lower branches sawn off. (2) Monumentale Eichen (Rainer Lippert), last update 10 March 2022: 'Stieleiche' (pedunculate oak), girth 5.91 m measured at waist height ('Taillenumfang'), height 27 m, crown about 28 m, 'etwa 200 Jahre', coordinates 50.097429, 8.794285. CONFLICTS: species (sessile vs pedunculate), age (380 vs about 200) and girth (608 vs 591 cm, different measuring heights). Age is not sharpened: given as the range, and the page should ask the reader to name the species. Only the flurbaum entry mentions three stems; do not state it as fact beyond 'one source says three-stemmed'. Alive: observed May 2026 by flurbaum.de (branch damage noted, no dieback noted). Park background: laid out from 1911 as Waldpark by Leonhard Eissnert (Regionalpark RheinMain); a tree this size predates the park, but no source says what the park did with it, so no bridge claim. Not a Naturdenkmal: the Offenbach list names the August-Reiss-Oak (frk_017) and Jahn Oak (frk_021) instead. Pin: two source coordinates about 30 m apart in a park, no crown identified, so approximate. No photograph checked; Commons geosearch within 150 m finds only 2013-era Panoramio uploads of unknown subject (File:Offenbach, Germany - panoramio - h4ck3rm1k3 (28).jpg is 26 m away), not verified as this tree.

trees.name: The Bethmannpark Ginkgo

location.address: Bethmannpark, Friedberger Landstrasse, Frankfurt

trees.access: Free, public city park (Bethmannpark); the register entry says publicly accessible. Park opening hours were not read (frankfurt.de returns 403).
trees.transport: Not verified. The park lies about 1 km east of the Konstablerwache area; tram stop Hessendenkmal is mapped about 120 m from the tree (Commons geotag), line numbers not checked.
trees.story:
Frankfurt's famous ginkgo is the one in Rödelheim that may have given Goethe two leaves for a poem. This one, in the Bethmannpark, is eight metres taller, and hardly anyone has written about it. Rainer Lippert, whose Monumentale Eichen site lists notable ginkgos, marks it as unknown in the literature.

What is known comes from a single visit. On 30 June 2015 the tree register at Baumkunde.de measured it at 4.84 metres round and 26 metres tall, gave its age as about 150 years and its condition as vital. Lippert's list carries the same figures from the same year, so that is one measurement repeated, not two that agree. Neither says at what height the tape went round, or whether the trunk is one stem or several.

The age is less settled than the size. The register says 150; other estimates run older, so we give it somewhere between 150 and 275 years and do not pick. No source connects this tree to Goethe. That story belongs to Rödelheim.

The 2015 entry is also the newest sign of life we have found, and we know of no photograph of it. The Bethmannpark is a free public park on the Friedberger Landstrasse, about a kilometre east of the Konstablerwache, and the Hessendenkmal tram stop is close by. The pin is approximate, so look for the fan-shaped leaves. If you have stood under it since 2015, tell us how it looks, and a photograph would settle it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped ginkgo leaves on a trunk 4.84 metres round, about 26 metres tall. It stands in the Bethmannpark, off the Friedberger Landstrasse near the Hessendenkmal tram stop.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn gold

trees.verify_notes: ONE MEASUREMENT CHAIN, flagged. Baumkunde.de register (Baumregister 189): girth 4.84 m 'gemessen' on 30 June 2015, height 26.0 m, age 150, condition 'vital', 'oeffentlich zugaenglich', coordinates N50 07.14' E8 41.3922' (about 50.1190, 8.6899). Rainer Lippert's Monumentale Eichen list (ginkgo page) carries the same figures (4.84 m, 26 m, about 150 years, year 2015), so it is the same measurement, not an independent one; it marks the tree as unknown in the literature. A monumentaltrees.com search snippet (page itself 403, not read, so only a pointer) gives a planting around 1800 +-50 and a possible multi-stem explanation for the large girth; that is why the age is a wide range here: 150 (register) to 275 (1800 +-50 would be 225 +-50). Do not sharpen. Whether the trunk is single or multi-stemmed is not stated by any fetched page; Baumkunde and Lippert do not give the measuring height. Alive: only the 2015 'vital' entry; lifecheck.py found no recent observation (nearest iNaturalist hit within range was an almond, not this tree), no Commons photograph of the ginkgo within 250 m. So alive-now is thin: flagged. Not the Goethe Ginkgo: that is the Roedelheim tree (frk_007); no source links Goethe to this one. Bethmannpark is about 3 ha, a protected monument since 1976 and bought by the city in 1941 (search snippet of frankfurt.de, not fetched). Pin: register coordinate in a 3 ha park, no crown identified, approximate. A park visit or reader GPS fix would settle both pin and condition.
